headline: AI Models Restate Files, Humans Own Promises in Docs
summary: A new pipeline ensures AI-generated documentation accurately reflects existing files, preventing models from making unsupported claims or promises.
details: AI-generated documentation can be a powerful tool, but it poses a risk when models make unsupported claims or promises. This article introduces a 'cite-or-drop' pipeline designed to enforce a clear distinction: AI models can restate checked-in facts, while humans retain ownership of promises, versions, and advice not directly sourced from existing files.

The pipeline operates in four stages: inventorying source artifacts, extracting candidate claims from AI drafts, binding each claim to a source root, and rejecting pull requests with unbound claims. This ensures that any sentence in model-touched documentation can be traced back to a specific file or source.

This approach prevents costly errors where AI might upgrade a beta feature status into a 'supported contract' without human oversight. Such misrepresentations can lead to support teams inheriting unfulfilled promises, causing significant revert costs after customers have already relied on the inaccurate information.

The system uses a checked-in bind map to define which source artifacts are permissible justifications for AI-generated prose. This map acts as a strict policy, limiting the model's access to specific files and preventing it from generating content based on conceptual essays or unverified information.

By splitting drafts into structured claim records, the pipeline allows continuous integration to flag specific problematic sentences without debating entire pages. This granular approach ensures that only verifiable facts are presented as restatements, while all commitments and unsupported advice remain under human purview.

headline: Google Keep adds long-awaited 'Find in note' feature
summary: The popular note-taking app finally gets a basic search functionality within notes, saving users from endless scrolling.
details: Google Keep, a staple for many users, has finally rolled out the 'Find in note' feature, a basic yet essential tool for navigating lengthy text within a single note.

Previously, Keep's search function only identified notes containing a specific term. Users had to manually scroll through the entire note to find the exact information, a process that could be time-consuming and frustrating, especially for long lists or detailed meeting notes.

The new 'Find in note' feature works much like 'Find in Page' on web browsers. Once a keyword is entered, Keep highlights all instances of that word within the note, allowing users to jump directly to the relevant sections.

This feature is particularly useful for power users who maintain extensive notes, such as detailed travel plans, recipes, or business meeting minutes. It eliminates the need to copy and paste entire notes into other applications like Google Docs for searching.

The 'Find in note' functionality began a limited rollout in early August 2026 and is available in version 5.26.3xx and above of the Google Keep app. Users who don't see the feature may need to update their app or try force-stopping it and clearing the cache.

While it's surprising that such a fundamental feature took over a decade to implement in an app as popular as Google Keep, its arrival significantly enhances the user experience and utility of the app, especially with its recent integration with Gemini.
